entries.e82e4bd02072c6eec1097cf5cdfa3e64de0162c4: <div sID="gen11752" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="72" osisID="Ps.72" sID="Ps.72"/> <div eID="gen11752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11753" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11754" type="x-p"/> The foregoing psalm was penned by David when he was old, and, it should seem, so was this too; for Solomon was now standing fair for the crown; that was his prayer for himself, this for his son and successor, and with these two the prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended, as we find in the close of this psalm. If we have but God's presence with us while we live, and good hopes concerning those that shall come after us that they shall be praising God on earth when we are praising him in heaven, it is enough. This is entitled "a psalm for Solomon:" it is probable that David dictated it, or, rather, that it was by the blessed Spirit dictated to him, when, a little before he died, by divine direction he settled the succession, and gave orders to proclaim Solomon king, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.30">1 Kings i. 30</reference>, &c. But, though Solomon's name is here made use of, Christ's kingdom is here prophesied of under the type and figure of Solomon's. David knew what the divine oracle was, That "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne," <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Acts ii. 30</reference>. To him he here bears witness, and with the prospect of the glories of his kingdom he comforted himself in his dying moments when he foresaw that his house would not be so with God, not so great not so good, as he wished. David, in spirit, I. Begins with a short prayer for his successor, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. He passes immediately into a long prediction of the glories of his reign, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2-Ps.72.17">ver. 2-17</reference>. And, III. He concludes with praise to the God of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.18-Ps.72.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. In singing this psalm we must have an eye to Christ, praising him as a King, and pleasing ourselves with our happiness as his subjects.
entries.803a073bdd3019dd6683a598322d1f072e63ccd6: <div eID="gen11754" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11753" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for Solomon.</title> <div sID="gen11755" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son. <div eID="gen11755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11756" type="x-p"/> This verse is a prayer for the king, even the king's son. <div eID="gen11756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11757" type="x-p"/> I. We may apply it to Solomon: <hi type="italic">Give him thy judgments, O God! and thy righteousness;</hi> make him a man, a king; make him a good man, a good king. 1. It is the prayer of a father for his child, a dying blessing, such as the patriarchs bequeathed to their children. The best thing we can ask of God for our children is that God will give them wisdom and grace to know and do their duty; that is better than gold. Solomon learned to pray for himself as his father had prayed for him, not that God would give him riches and honour, but a wise and understanding heart. It was a comfort to David that his own son was to be his successor, but more so that he was likely to be both judicious and righteous. David had given him a good education (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.3">Prov. iv. 3</reference>), had taught him <hi type="italic">good judgment and righteous,</hi> yet that would not do unless God gave him his judgments. Parents cannot give grace to their children, but may by prayer bring them to the God of grace, and shall not seek him in vain, for their prayer shall either be answered or it shall return with comfort into their own bosom. 2. It is the prayer of a king for his successor. David had executed judgment and justice during his reign, and now he prays that his son might do so too. Such a concern as this we should have for posterity, desiring and endeavouring that those who come after us may do God more and better service in their day than we have done in ours. Those have little love either to God or man, and are of a very narrow selfish spirit, who care not what becomes of the world and the church when they are gone. 3. It is the prayer of subjects for their king. It should seem, David penned this psalm for the use of the people, that they, in singing, might pray for Solomon. Those who would live quiet and peaceable lives must pray for kings and all in authority, that God would give them his judgments and righteousness. <div eID="gen11757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11758" type="x-p"/> II. We may apply it to Christ; not that he who intercedes for us needs us to intercede for him; but, 1. It is a prayer of the Old-Testament church for sending the Messiah, as the church's King, King <hi type="italic">on the holy hill of Zion,</hi> of whom the King of kings had said, <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6-Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 6, 7</reference>. "Hasten his coming to whom all judgment is committed;" and we must thus hasten the second coming of Christ, when he shall <hi type="italic">judge the world in righteousness.</hi> 2. It is an expression of the satisfaction which all true believers take in the authority which the Lord Jesus has received from the Father: "Let him have all power both in heaven and earth, and be the Lord our righteousness; let him be the great trustee of divine grace for all that are his; give it to him, that he may give it to us."
entries.3558727356d6854cdd975b5de504682b64188ce0: <div eID="gen11758" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Kingdom of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen11759" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment. <hi type="super">3</hi> The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness. <hi type="super">4</hi> He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor. <hi type="super">5</hi> They shall fear thee as long as the sun and moon endure, throughout all generations. <hi type="super">6</hi> He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers <hi type="italic">that</hi> water the earth. <hi type="super">7</hi> In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth. <hi type="super">8</hi> He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth. <hi type="super">9</hi> They that dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him; and his enemies shall lick the dust. <hi type="super">10</hi> The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. <hi type="super">11</hi> Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him. <hi type="super">12</hi> For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and <hi type="italic">him</hi> that hath no helper. <hi type="super">13</hi> He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the needy. <hi type="super">14</hi> He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he shall live, and to him shall be given of the gold of Sheba: prayer also shall be made for him continually; <hi type="italic">and</hi> daily shall he be praised. <hi type="super">16</hi> There shall be a handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon: and <hi type="italic">they</hi> of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> His name shall endure for ever: his name shall be continued as long as the sun: and <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall be blessed in him: all nations shall call him blessed. <div eID="gen11759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11760" type="x-p"/> This is a prophecy of the prosperity and perpetuity of the kingdom of Christ under the shadow of the reign of Solomon. It comes in, 1. As a plea to enforce the prayer: "Lord, <hi type="italic">give him thy judgments and thy righteousness,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">he shall judge thy people with righteousness,</hi> and so shall answer the end of his elevation, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">v. 2</reference>. Give him thy grace, and then thy people, committed to his charge, will have the benefit of it." <hi type="italic">Because God loved Israel, he made him king over them to do judgment and justice,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.8">2 Chron. ix. 8</reference>. We may in faith wrestle with God for that grace which we have reason to think will be of common advantage to his church. 2. As an answer of peace to the prayer. As by the prayer of faith we return answers to God's promises of mercy, so by the promises of mercy God returns answers to our prayers of faith. That this prophecy must refer to the kingdom of the Messiah is plain, because there are many passages in it which cannot be applied to the reign of Solomon. There was indeed a great deal of righteousness and peace, at first, in the administration of his government; but, before the end of his reign, there were both trouble and unrighteousness. The kingdom here spoken of is to last as long as the sun, but Solomon's was soon extinct. Therefore even the Jewish expositors understand it of the kingdom of the Messiah. <div eID="gen11760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11761" type="x-p"/> Let us observe the many great and precious promises here made, which were to have their full accomplishment only in the kingdom of Christ; and yet some of them were in part fulfilled in Solomon's reign. <div eID="gen11761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11762" type="x-p"/> I. That it should be a <hi type="italic">righteous government</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall judge thy people with righteousness.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa. xi. 4</reference>. All the laws of Christ's kingdom are consonant to the eternal rules of equity; the chancery it erects to relieve against the rigours of the broken law is indeed a court of equity; and against the sentence of his last judgment there will lie no exception. The peace of his kingdom shall be supported by righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">v. 3</reference>); for then only is the peace like a river, when the <hi type="italic">righteousness is as the waves of the sea.</hi> The world will be judged in righteousness, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Acts xvii. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen11762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11763" type="x-p"/> II. That it should be a peaceable government: <hi type="italic">The mountains shall bring peace, and the little hills</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">v. 3</reference>); that is (says Dr. Hammond), both the superior and the inferior courts of judicature in Solomon's kingdom. There shall be <hi type="italic">abundance of peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">v. 7</reference>. Solomon's name signifies <hi type="italic">peaceable,</hi> and such was his reign; for in it Israel enjoyed the victories of the foregoing reign and preserved the tranquillity and repose of that reign. But peace is, in a special manner, the glory of Christ's kingdom; for, as far as it prevails, it reconciles men to God, to themselves, and to one another, and slays all enmities; for he is our peace. <div eID="gen11763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11764" type="x-p"/> III. That the poor and needy should be, in a particular manner, taken under the protection of this government: <hi type="italic">He shall judge thy poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">v. 2</reference>. Those are God's poor that are impoverished by keeping a good conscience, and those shall be provided for with a distinguishing care, shall be judged for with judgment, with a particular cognizance taken of their case and a particular vengeance taken for their wrongs. <hi type="italic">The poor of the people,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the children of the needy,</hi> he will be sure so to judge as to save, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">v. 4</reference>. This is insisted upon again (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.12-Ps.72.13">v. 12, 13</reference>), intimating that Christ will be sure to carry his cause on behalf of his injured poor. <hi type="italic">He will deliver the needy</hi> that lie at the mercy of their oppressors, <hi type="italic">the poor also,</hi> both because they have <hi type="italic">no helper</hi> and it is for his honour to help them and because they cry unto him and he has promised, in answer to their prayers, to help them; they by prayer <hi type="italic">commit themselves unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Ps. x. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">He will spare the needy</hi> that throw themselves on his mercy, and will not be rigorous and severe with them; he <hi type="italic">will save their souls,</hi> and that is all they desire. <hi type="italic">Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.</hi> Christ is the poor man's King. <div eID="gen11764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11765" type="x-p"/> IV. That proud oppressors shall be reckoned with: <hi type="italic">He shall break them in pieces</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">v. 4</reference>), shall take away their power to hurt, and punish them for all the mischief they have done. This is the office of a good king, <hi type="italic">Parcere subjectis, et debellare superbos—To spare the vanquished and debase the proud.</hi> The devil is the great oppressor, whom Christ will break in pieces and of whose kingdom he will be the destruction. <hi type="italic">With the breath of his mouth shall he slay that wicked one</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa. xi. 4</reference>), and shall deliver the souls of his people <hi type="italic">from deceit and violence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">v. 14</reference>. He shall save from the power of Satan, both as an old serpent working by deceit to ensnare them and as a roaring lion working by violence to terrify and devour them. So <hi type="italic">precious shall their blood be unto him</hi> that not a drop of it shall be shed, by the deceit or violence of Satan or his instruments, without being reckoned for. Christ is a King, who, though he calls his subjects sometimes to resist unto blood for him, yet is not prodigal of their blood, nor will ever have it parted with but upon a valuable consideration to his glory and theirs, and the filling up of the measure of their enemies' iniquity. <div eID="gen11765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11766" type="x-p"/> V. That religion shall flourish under Christ's government (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall fear thee as long as the sun and moon endure.</hi> Solomon indeed built the temple, and the fear and worship of God were well kept up, for some time, under his government, but it did not last long; this therefore must point at Christ's kingdom, all the subjects of which are brought to and kept in the fear of God; for the Christian religion has a direct tendency to, and a powerful influence upon, the support and advancement of natural religion. Faith in Christ will set up, and keep up, the fear of God; and therefore this is the everlasting gospel that is preached, <hi type="italic">Fear God, and give honour to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 7</reference>. And, as Christ's government promotes devotion towards God, so it promotes both justice and charity among men (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">In his days shall the righteous flourish;</hi> righteousness shall be practised, and those that practise righteousness shall be preferred. Righteousness shall abound and be in reputation, shall command and be in power. The law of Christ, written in the heart, disposes men to be honest and just, and to render to all their due; it likewise disposes men to live in love, and so it produces abundance of peace and beats swords into ploughshares. Both holiness and love shall be perpetual in Christ's kingdom, and shall never go to decay, for the subjects of it shall <hi type="italic">fear God as long as the sun and moon endure;</hi> Christianity, in the profession of it, having got footing in the world, shall keep its ground till the end of time, and having, in the power of it, got footing in the heart, it will continue there till, by death, the sun, and the moon, and the stars (that is, the bodily senses) are darkened. Through all the changes of the world, and all the changes of life, Christ's kingdom will support itself; and, if the fear of God continue as long as the sun and moon, abundance of peace will. The peace of the church, the peace of the soul, shall run parallel with its purity and piety, and last as long as these last. <div eID="gen11766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11767" type="x-p"/> VI. That Christ's government shall be very comfortable to all his faithful loving subjects (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall,</hi> by the graces and comforts of his Spirit, <hi type="italic">come down like rain upon the mown grass;</hi> not on that which is cut down, but that which is left growing, that it may spring again, though it was beheaded. The gospel of Christ distils as the rain, which softens the ground that was hard, moistens that which was dry, and so makes it green and fruitful, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10">Isa. lv. 10</reference>. Let our hearts <hi type="italic">drink in the rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.7">Heb. vi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen11767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11768" type="x-p"/> VII. That Christ's kingdom shall be extended very far, and greatly enlarged; considering, <div eID="gen11768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11769" type="x-p"/> 1. The extent of his territories (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall have dominion from sea to sea</hi> (from the South Sea to the North, or from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean) <hi type="italic">and from the river</hi> Euphrates, or Nile, <hi type="italic">to the ends of the earth.</hi> Solomon's dominion was very large (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1 Kings iv. 21</reference>), according to the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen. xv. 18</reference>. But no sea, no river, is named, that it might, by these proverbial expressions, intimate the universal monarchy of the Lord Jesus. His gospel has been, or shall be, preached <hi type="italic">to all nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">Matt. xxiv. 14</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">kingdoms of the world</hi> shall <hi type="italic">become his kingdoms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev. xi. 15</reference>) when the fulness of the Gentiles shall be brought in. His territories shall be extended to those countries, (1.) That were strangers to him: <hi type="italic">Those that dwell in the wilderness,</hi> out of all high roads, that seldom hear news, shall hear the glad tidings of the Redeemer and redemption by him, <hi type="italic">shall bow before him,</hi> shall believe in him, accept of him, worship him, and take his yoke upon them. Before the Lord Jesus we must all either bow or break; if we break, we are ruined—if we bow, we are certainly made for ever. (2.) That were enemies to him, and had fought against him: <hi type="italic">They shall lick the dust;</hi> they shall be brought down and laid in the dust, shall bite the ground for vexation, and be so hunger-bitten that they shall be glad of dust, the serpent's meat (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>), for of his seed they are; and over whom shall not he rule, when his enemies themselves are thus humbled and brought low? <div eID="gen11769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11770" type="x-p"/> 2. The dignity of his tributaries. He shall not only reign over those that dwell in the wilderness, the peasants and cottagers, but over those that dwell in the palaces (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The kings of Tarshish, and of the isles,</hi> that lie most remote from Israel and are <hi type="italic">the isles of the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen. x. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">shall bring presents</hi> to him as their sovereign Lord, by and under whom they hold their crowns and all their crown lands. They shall court his favour, and make an interest in him, that they may hear his wisdom. This was literally fulfilled in Solomon (for <hi type="italic">all the kings of the earth sought the wisdom of Solomon, and brought every man his present,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.23-2Chr.9.24">2 Chron. ix. 23, 24</reference>), and in Christ too, when the wise men of the east, who probably were men of the first rank in their own country, came to worship him and <hi type="italic">brought him presents,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.2.11">Matt. ii. 11</reference>. They shall present themselves to him; that is the best present we can bring to Christ, and without that no other present is acceptable, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Rom. xii. 1</reference>. They <hi type="italic">shall offer gifts,</hi> spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise, offer them to Christ as their God, on Christ as their altar, which sanctifies every gift. Their conversion to God is called the <hi type="italic">offering up,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sacrificing, of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Rom. xv. 16</reference>. Yea, all kings shall, sooner or later, <hi type="italic">fall down before him,</hi> either to do their duty to him or to receive their doom from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">v. 11</reference>. They shall fall before him, either as his willing subjects or as his conquered captives, as suppliants for his mercy or expectants of his judgment. And, when the kings submit, the people come in of course: <hi type="italic">All nations shall serve him;</hi> all shall be invited into his service; some of all nations shall come into it, and in every nation <hi type="italic">incense shall be offered to him and a pure offering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen11770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11771" type="x-p"/> VIII. That he shall be honoured and beloved by all his subjects (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall live;</hi> his subjects shall desire his life (<hi type="italic">O king! live for ever</hi>) and with good reason; for he has said, <hi type="italic">Because I live, you shall live also; and of him it is witnessed that he liveth, ever liveth, making intercession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.8">Heb. vii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">25</reference>. He shall live, and live prosperously; and, 1. Presents shall be made to him. Though he shall be able to live without them, for he needs neither the gifts nor the services of any, yet to him <hi type="italic">shall be given of the gold of Sheba</hi>—gold, the best of metals, gold of Sheba, which probably was the finest gold; for he that is best must be served with the best. Those that have abundance of the wealth of this world, that have gold at command, must give it to Christ, must serve him with it, do good with it. <hi type="italic">Honour the Lord with thy substance.</hi> 2. Prayers shall be made for him, and that continually. The people prayed for Solomon, and that helped to make him and his reign so great a blessing to them. It is the duty of subjects to make prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, for kings and all in authority, not in compliment to them, as is too often done, but in concern for the public welfare. But how is this applied to Christ? He needs not our prayers, nor can have any benefit by them. But the Old-Testament saints prayed for his coming, prayed continually for it; for they called him, <hi type="italic">He that should come.</hi> And now that he has come we must pray for the success of his gospel and the advancement of his kingdom, which he calls praying for him (Hosanna to the Son of David, prosperity to his reign), and we must pray for his second coming. It may be read, <hi type="italic">Prayer shall be made through him,</hi> or for his sake; whatsoever we ask of the Father shall be in his name and in dependence upon his intercession. 3. Praises shall be made of him, and high encomiums given of his wisdom, justice, and goodness: <hi type="italic">Daily shall he be praised.</hi> By praying daily in his name we give him honour. Subjects ought to speak well of the government that is a blessing to them; and much more ought all Christians to praise Jesus Christ, daily to praise him; for they owe their all to him, and to him they lie under the highest obligations. <div eID="gen11771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11772" type="x-p"/> IX. That under his government there shall be a wonderful increase both of meat and mouths, both of the fruits of the earth in the country and of the people inhabiting the cities, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.16">v. 16</reference>. 1. The country shall grow rich. Sow but a <hi type="italic">handful of corn on the top of the mountains,</hi> whence one would expect but little, and yet <hi type="italic">the fruit of it shall shake like Lebanon;</hi> it shall come up like a wood, so thick, and tall, and strong, like the cedars of Lebanon. Even upon the tops of the mountains the earth shall bring forth by handfuls; that is an expression of great plenty (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.47">Gen. xli. 47</reference>), as the grass upon the house top is said to be that wherewith the mower fills not his hand. This is applicable to the wonderful productions of the seed of the gospel in the days of the Messiah. A handful of that seed, sown in the mountainous and barren soil of the Gentile world, produced a wonderful harvest gathered in to Christ, fruit that shook like Lebanon. The fields were <hi type="italic">white to the harvest,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.35">John iv. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.37">Matt. ix. 37</reference>. The grain of mustard-seed grew up to a great tree. 2. The towns shall grow populous: <hi type="italic">Those of the city shall flourish like grass,</hi> for number, for verdure. The gospel church, the city of God among men, shall have all the marks of prosperity, many shall be added to it, and those that are shall be happy in it. <div eID="gen11772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11773" type="x-p"/> X. That his government shall be perpetual, both to his honour and to the happiness of his subjects. The Lord Jesus shall reign for ever, and of him only this must be understood, and not at all of Solomon. It is Christ only that shall <hi type="italic">be feared throughout all generations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.5">v. 5</reference>) and <hi type="italic">as long as the sun and moon endure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">v. 7</reference>. 1. The honour of the princes is immortal and shall never be sullied (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">His name shall endure for ever,</hi> in spite of all the malicious attempts and endeavours of the powers of darkness to eclipse the lustre of it and to cut off the line of it; it shall be preserved; it shall be perpetuated; it shall be propagated. As the names of earthly princes are continued in their posterity, so Christ's in himself. <hi type="italic">Filiabitur nomen ejus—His name shall descend to posterity.</hi> All nations, while the world stands, shall call him blessed, shall bless God for him, continually speak well of him, and think themselves happy in him. To the end of time, and to eternity, his name shall be celebrated, shall be made use of; every tongue shall confess it and every knee shall bow before it. 2. The happiness of the people if universal too; it is complete and everlasting: <hi type="italic">Men shall be blessed,</hi> truly and for ever blessed, <hi type="italic">in him.</hi> This plainly refers to the promise made unto the fathers that in the Messiah all the nations of the earth should be blessed. <reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen. xii. 3</reference>.
entries.6501e696344f44867ebfcee2ade28af476c35a95: <div eID="gen11773" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Thanksgiving and Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen11774" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things. <hi type="super">19</hi> And blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> his glorious name for ever: and let the whole earth be filled <hi type="italic">with</hi> his glory; Amen, and Amen. <hi type="super">20</hi> The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended. <div eID="gen11774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11775" type="x-p"/> Such an illustrious prophecy as is in the foregoing verses of the Messiah and his kingdom may fitly be concluded, as it is here, with hearty prayers and praises. <div eID="gen11775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11776" type="x-p"/> I. The psalmist is here enlarged in thanksgivings for the prophecy and promise, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.18-Ps.72.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. So sure is every word of God, and with so much satisfaction may we rely upon it, that we have reason enough to give thanks for what he has said, though it be not yet done. We must own that for all the great things he has done for the world, for the church, for the children of men, for his own children, in the kingdom of providence, in the kingdom of grace, for all the power and trust lodged in the hands of the Redeemer, God is worthy to be praised; we must stir up ourselves and all that is within us to praise him after the best manner, and desire that all others may do it. <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">blessed be his glorious name;</hi> for it is only in his name that we can contribute any thing to his glory and blessedness, and yet that is also <hi type="italic">exalted above all blessing and praise.</hi> Let it be blessed for ever, it shall be blessed for ever, it deserves to be blessed for ever, and we hope to be forever blessing it. We are here taught to bless the name of Christ, and to bless God in Christ, for all that which he has done for us by him. We must bless him, 1. As the Lord God, as a self-existent self-sufficient Being, and our sovereign Lord. 2. As the God of Israel, in covenant with that people and worshipped by them, and who does this in performance of the truth unto Jacob and the mercy to Abraham, 3. As the God <hi type="italic">who only does wondrous things,</hi> in creation and providence, and especially this work of redemption, which excels them all. Men's works are little, common, trifling things, and even these they could not do without him. But God does all by his own power, and they are wondrous things which he does, and such as will be the eternal admiration of saints and angels. <div eID="gen11776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11777" type="x-p"/> II. He is earnest in prayer for the accomplishment of this prophecy and promise: <hi type="italic">Let the whole earth be filled with his glory,</hi> as it will be when the <hi type="italic">kings of Tarshish, and the isles, shall bring presents to him.</hi> It is sad to think how empty the earth is of the glory of God, how little service and honour he has from a world to which he is such a bountiful benefactor. All those, therefore, that wish well to the honour of God and the welfare of mankind, cannot but desire that the earth may be filled with the discoveries of his glory, suitably returned in thankful acknowledgments of his glory. Let every heart, and every mouth, and every assembly, be filled with the high praises of God. We shall see how earnest David is in this prayer, and how much his heart is in it, if we observe, 1. How he shuts up the prayer with a double seal: "<hi type="italic">Amen and amen;</hi> again and again I say, I say it and let all others say the same, so be it. Amen to my prayer; Amen to the prayers of all the saints to this purport—<hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come.</hi>" 2. How he ever shuts up his life with this prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">v. 20</reference>. This was the last psalm that ever he penned, though not placed last in this collection; he penned it when he lay on his death-bed, and with this he breathes his last: "Let God be glorified, let the kingdom of the Messiah be set up, and kept up, in the world, and I have enough, I desire no more. With this let <hi type="italic">the prayers of David the son of Jesse</hi> be <hi type="italic">ended.</hi> Even so, come, Lord Jesus, come quickly."  <chapter eID="Ps.72"/> <div eID="gen11777" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b338d47e2760f0d02314ca2d436fc01b33ace78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6291"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 72</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.72.1-Ps.72.19">Psa 72:1-19</reference>. For, or literally, "of Solomon." The closing verse rather relates to the second book of Psalms, of which this is the last, and was perhaps added by some collector, to intimate that the collection, to which, as chief author, David's name was appended, was closed. In this view, these may consistently be the productions of others included, as of Asaph, sons of Korah, and Solomon; and a few of David's may be placed in the latter series. The fact that here the usual mode of denoting authorship is used, is strongly conclusive that Solomon was the author, especially as no stronger objection appears than what has been now set aside. The Psalm, in highly wrought figurative style, describes the reign of a king as "righteous, universal, beneficent, and perpetual." By the older Jewish and most modern Christian interpreters, it has been referred to Christ, whose reign, present and prospective, alone corresponds with its statements. As the imagery of the second Psalm was drawn from the martial character of David's reign, that of this is from the peaceful and prosperous state of Solomon's.</title> <div sID="gen9624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6291"/><hi type="bold">1. Give the king, &c.--</hi>a prayer which is equivalent to a prediction.<div eID="gen9624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgments--</hi>the acts, and (figuratively) the principles of a right government (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.39">9:39</reference>).<div eID="gen9625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>qualifications for conducting such a government.<div eID="gen9626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king's son--</hi>same person as a king--a very proper title for Christ, as such in both natures.<div eID="gen9627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9628" type="x-p"/> 2, &c. The effects of such a government by one thus endowed are detailed.<div eID="gen9628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy people ... and thy poor--</hi>or, "meek," the pious subjects of his government. <div eID="gen9629" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fcc571185e1c70aa305b04ae555541de759ceca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6292"/><div sID="gen9630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6292"/>3. As mountains and hills are not usually productive, they are here selected to show the abundance of peace, being represented as<div eID="gen9630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bringing--</hi>or, literally, "bearing" it as a produce.<div eID="gen9631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by righteousness--</hi>that is, by means of his eminently just and good methods of ruling. <div eID="gen9632" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed310af8249a79a0ca0c457a401291d6f9d81ecb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6293"/><div sID="gen9633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6293"/>4. That peace, including prosperity, as an eminent characteristic of Christ's reign (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">11:9</reference>), will be illustrated in the security provided for the helpless and needy, and the punishment inflicted on oppressors, whose power to injure or mar the peace of others will be destroyed (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">Is 65:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">Zec 9:10</reference>).<div eID="gen9633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of the needy--</hi>for the needy (compare sons of strangers, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.45">Psa 18:45</reference> [Margin]). <div eID="gen9634" type="x-p"/>
entries.de2900efea3d81b0613cdbc5de77600af325b2b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6294"/><div sID="gen9635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6294"/><hi type="bold">5. as long as ... endure--</hi>literally, "with the sun," coeval with its existence, and before, or, in presence of the moon, while it lasts (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.11.28">Ge 11:28</reference>, "before Terah," literally, "in presence of," while he lived). <div eID="gen9635" type="x-p"/>
entries.294f4799bbb9a9cdd516e764de640fa79efebdff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6295"/><div sID="gen9636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6295"/>6. A beautiful figure expresses the grateful nature of His influence;<div eID="gen9636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9637" type="x-p"/> 7, and, carrying out the figure, the results are described in an abundant production.<div eID="gen9637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the righteous--</hi>literally, "righteousness."<div eID="gen9638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flourish--</hi>literally, "sprout," or, "spring forth." <div eID="gen9639" type="x-p"/>
entries.65a901084ef7915ade8c98e712245b24ed80f078: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6296"/><div sID="gen9640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6296"/>8. The foreign nations mentioned (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.9">Psa 72:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">10</reference>) could not be included in the limits, if designed to indicate the boundaries of Solomon's kingdom. The terms, though derived from those used (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.31">Ex 23:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.24">De 11:24</reference>) to denote the possessions of Israel, must have a wider sense. Thus, "ends of the earth" is never used of Palestine, but always of the world (compare Margin). <div eID="gen9640" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab3706b24476631980cf71588027fb078380af09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6297"/><div sID="gen9641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6297"/>9-11. The extent of the conquests.<div eID="gen9641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They that dwell in the wilderness--</hi>the wild, untutored tribes of deserts.<div eID="gen9642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow ... dust--</hi>in profound submission. The remotest and wealthiest nations shall acknowledge Him (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.45.12">Psa 45:12</reference>). <div eID="gen9643" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1f6171a704bb6ab48578528a8fba558b55cc7fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6298"/><div sID="gen9644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6298"/>12-14. They are not the conquests of arms, but the influences of humane and peaceful principles (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Is 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.9">11:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen9644" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8e297279f0a55eb9aa6eaf04b8fc23e15c979c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6299"/><div sID="gen9645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6299"/>15. In his prolonged life he will continue to receive the honorable gifts of the rich, and the prayers of his people shall be made for him, and their praises given to him. <div eID="gen9645" type="x-p"/>
entries.67a2a999d63f4138ec03b6dd06e7275e7cd9ad01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6300"/><div sID="gen9646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6300"/>16. The spiritual blessings, as often in Scripture, are set forth by material, the abundance of which is described by a figure, in which a "handful" (or literally, "a piece," or small portion) of corn in the most unpropitious locality, shall produce a crop, waving in the wind in its luxuriant growth, like the forests of Lebanon.<div eID="gen9646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they of the city ... earth--</hi>This clause denotes the rapid and abundant increase of population--<div eID="gen9647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9648" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>or, "from"<div eID="gen9648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city--</hi>Jerusalem, the center and seat of the typical kingdom.<div eID="gen9649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flourish--</hi>or, glitter as new grass--that is, bloom. This increase corresponds with the increased productiveness. So, as the gospel blessings are diffused, there shall arise increasing recipients of them, out of the Church in which Christ resides as head. <div eID="gen9650" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d1d846355ed69096fc6c569a4afad0d2d79378a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6301"/><div sID="gen9651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6301"/><hi type="bold">17. His name--</hi>or, "glorious perfections."<div eID="gen9651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as long as the sun--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.72.5">Psa 72:5</reference>).<div eID="gen9652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men shall be blessed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.18">18:18</reference>). <div eID="gen9653" type="x-p"/>
entries.82df6c0ce3aa5d83feb1c2ec8567a17e84742c0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6302"/><div sID="gen9654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6302"/>18-19. These words close the Psalm in terms consistent with the style of the context, while <reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">Psa 72:20</reference> is evidently, from its prosaic style, an addition for the purpose above explained [see on Psa 72:1]. <div eID="gen9654" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd8446a3517e7735b1eb78f08d06fab34d13e057: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6303"/><div sID="gen9655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6303"/><hi type="bold">20. ended--</hi>literally, "finished," or completed; the word never denotes fulfilment, except in a very late usage, as in <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1">Ezr 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Da 12:7</reference>. <chapter eID="Ps.72"/>

entries.d71766dffc67f5f875063274e296e3635aa57dd4: <div eID="gen20895" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20896" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20897" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20897" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20896" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20898" type="x-p"/> David prays to God for Solomon, <reference osisRef="Psa.72.1">Psa 72:1</reference>; prescribes Solomon's work, <reference osisRef="Psa.72.2">Psa 72:2</reference>; the effects of his administration, <reference osisRef="Psa.72.3-Psa.72.7">Psa 72:3-7</reference>; the extent of his dominion, <reference osisRef="Psa.72.8-Psa.72.11">Psa 72:8-11</reference>; his mercy and kindness to the poor, and the perpetuity of his praise, <reference osisRef="Psa.72.12-Psa.72.17">Psa 72:12-17</reference>. God is blessed for his power and goodness; and the psalmist prays that the whole earth may be filled with his glory, <reference osisRef="Psa.72.18-Psa.72.20">Psa 72:18-20</reference>. <div eID="gen20898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20899" type="x-p"/> The title לשלמה lishelomoh, we translate, A Psalm for Solomon. The Chaldee says, "By the hand of Solomon, spoken prophetically." The Syriac, "A Psalm of David, when he had constituted Solomon king." All the other Versions attribute it to Solomon himself. But in the conclusion of the Psalm it appears to be attributed to David. "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended." It is most probably a Psalm of David, composed in his last days, when he had set this beloved son on the throne of the kingdom. "Then," says Calmet, "transported with joy and gratitude, he addressed this Psalm to God, in which he prays him to pour out his blessings on the young king, and upon the people. He then, wrapped up in a Divine enthusiasm, ascends to a higher subject; and sings the glory of the Messiah, and the magnificence of his reign. Hence it is that we may see in this Psalm a great number of expressions which cannot relate to Solomon, unless in a hyperbolical and figurative sense; but, applied to Christ, they are literally and rigorously exact." <div eID="gen20899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20900" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20901" type="x-p"/> Give the king thy judgments - Let Solomon receive thy law, as the civil and ecclesiastical code by which he is to govern the kingdom. <div eID="gen20901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20902" type="x-p"/> And thy righteousness unto the king's son - Righteousness may signify equity. Let him not only rule according to the strict letter of thy law, that being the base on which all his decisions shall be founded; but let him rule also according to equity, that rigorous justice may never become oppressive. Solomon is called here the king, because now set upon the Jewish throne; and he is called the king's son, to signify his right to that throne on which he now sat.
entries.e45bad6d9ad2e2d0401c57a8493485ccd73bb9f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20903" type="x-p"/> He shall judge thy people with righteousness - With justice and mercy mixed, or according to equity. <div eID="gen20903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20904" type="x-p"/> And thy poor with judgment - Every one according to the law which thou hast appointed; but with especial tenderness to the poor and afflicted.
entries.716a03504911cbf06d57b7f43d56aa4807bac768: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20905" type="x-p"/> The mountains shall bring peace - Perhaps mountains and hills are here taken in their figurative sense, to signify princes and petty governors; and it is a prediction that all governors of provinces and magistrates should administer equal justice in their several departments and jurisdictions; so that universal peace should be preserved, and the people be every where prosperous; for שלום shalom signifies both peace and prosperity, for without the former the latter never existed. <div eID="gen20905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20906" type="x-p"/> But what is the meaning of "the little hills by righteousness?" Why, it has no meaning: and it has none, because it is a false division of the verse. The word בצדקה bitsedakah, in righteousness, at the end of <reference osisRef="Psa.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference>, should begin <reference osisRef="Psa.72.4">Psa 72:4</reference>, and then the sense will be plain. <reference osisRef="Psa.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference> : "The mountains and the hills shall bring prosperity to the people." <reference osisRef="Psa.72.4">Psa 72:4</reference> : "In righteousness he shall judge the poor of the people: he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor." <div eID="gen20906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20907" type="x-p"/> The effects, mentioned in the fourth verse, show that King Solomon should act according to the law of his God; and that all officers, magistrates, and governors, should minister equal rights through every part of the land. The Septuagint has the true division: Αναλαβετω τα ορη ειρηνην τῳ λαῳ σου, και οἱ βουνοι· Εν δικαιοσυνῃ κρινει τους πτωχους του λαου, κ. τ. λ. "The mountains shall bring peace to thy people, and the hills: In righteousness shall he judge the poor of thy people," etc.
entries.eb3e401e00be74661d3530b7b2891b068acddb0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20908" type="x-p"/> They shall fear thee - There is no sense in which this can be spoken of Solomon, nor indeed of any other man: it belongs to Jesus Christ, and to him alone. He is the Prance of peace, who shall be feared and reverenced "through all generations, and as long as the sun and moon endure."
entries.3e89d368fe9b660614adf2360e054865a111fb0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20909" type="x-p"/> He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass - The word גז gez, which we translate mown grass, more properly means pastured grass or pastured land; for the dew of the night is intended to restore the grass which has been eaten in the course of the day. This very idea the Chaldee has seized, and renders the place thus: "He shall descend gently, like rain upon the grass which has been eaten by the locust." But there seems to be a reference to the thick night dews which in summer fall on the pasturages, and become the means of restoring the grass consumed in the day-time by the cattle. This is finely expressed by the most accomplished of all poets and agriculturists: - <div eID="gen20909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20910" type="x-p"/> Et quantum longis carpent armenta diebus, <div eID="gen20910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20911" type="x-p"/> Exigua tantum gelidus ros nocte reponet. <div eID="gen20911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20912" type="x-p"/> Virg. Geor. ii., ver. 201. "For what the day devours, the nightly dew <div eID="gen20912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20913" type="x-p"/> Shall to the morn by pearly drops renew." <div eID="gen20913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20914" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen20914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20915" type="x-p"/> Or to leave poetry, which always says too much or too little, the plain prose is: - "And as much as the flocks crop in the long days, <div eID="gen20915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20916" type="x-p"/> So much shall the cold dew restore in one short night." <div eID="gen20916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20917" type="x-p"/> As showers that water the earth - The influence of the doctrine and Spirit of Christ on the soul of man shall be as grateful, as refreshing, and as fructifying, as the nightly dews on the cropped fields, and the vernal showers on the cultivated lands. Without his influence all tillage is vain; without him there can neither be seed nor fruit.
entries.69b7a23a77f7e333102fde81b52b46150055f457: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20918" type="x-p"/> In his days shall the righteous flourish - There was nothing but peace and prosperity all the days of Solomon: for, "In his days Judah and Israel dwelt safely; every man under his vine and under his fig-tree, from Dan even to Beersheba;" <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">1Kgs 4:25</reference>. <div eID="gen20918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20919" type="x-p"/> So long as the moon endureth - עד בלי ירח ad beli yareach, "Till there be no more moon."
entries.962afbc835dff01d794b011b9faa92ddac32402a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20920" type="x-p"/> He shall have dominion also from sea to sea - The best comment on this, as it refers to Solomon, may be found in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1Kgs 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.24">1Kgs 4:24</reference> : "And Solomon reigned over all kingdoms, from the river unto the land of the Philistines, and unto the border of Egypt; for he had dominion over all on this side the river, from Tiphsah even to Azzah, over all the kings on this side the river; and he had peace on all sides round about him." <div eID="gen20920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20921" type="x-p"/> Solomon, it appears, reigned over all the provinces from the river Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, even to the frontiers of Egypt. The Euphrates was on the east of Solomon's dominions; the Philistines were westward, on the Mediterranean sea; and Egypt was on the south. Solomon had therefore, as tributaries, the kingdoms of Syria, Damascus, Moab, and Ammon, which lay between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean. Thus he appears to have possessed all the land which God covenanted with Abraham to give to his posterity. <div eID="gen20921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20922" type="x-p"/> Unto the ends of the earth - Or land, must mean the tract of country along the Mediterranean sea, which was the boundary of the land on that side: but, as the words may refer to Christ, every thing may be taken in its utmost latitude and extent.
entries.4bef7529995c773a5fc0d6bb525c2c79ab88dc64: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20923" type="x-p"/> They that dwell in the wilderness - The ציים tsiyim, termed Ethiopians by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic. The Syriac terms them the islands. But it is likely that those who dwell by the sea-coasts, and support themselves by navigation and fishing, are here intended. <div eID="gen20923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20924" type="x-p"/> His enemies shall lick the dust - Shall be so completely subdued, that they shall be reduced to the most abject state of vassalage, till they shall become proselytes to the Jewish faith.
entries.556cb84fac280b1348d4f69190a8f5c7aa1b501d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20925" type="x-p"/> The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shalt bring presents - Though Solomon did not reign over Cilicia, of which Tarsus was the capital, yet he might receive gifts, not in the sense of tribute; for מנחה minchah, the word here used, signifies a gratitude or friendly offering. <div eID="gen20925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20926" type="x-p"/> The kings of Sheba and Seba - Both countries of Arabia. From the former came the queen of Sheba, to hear the wisdom of Solomon. And she brought exceeding great presents or gifts, but not in the way of tribute, for Solomon had no jurisdiction in her country. And certainly many sovereigns, to obtain his friendship, sent him various presents of the choicest produce of their respective countries; and no doubt he did with them as with the queen of Sheba, gave them gifts in return. Hence the word אשכר eshcar is used, which signifies "a compensative present, made on account of benefits received."
entries.a1b26b0364bec470928f7d2a63b6669ec8408359: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20927" type="x-p"/> All kings shall fall down before - They shall reverence him on account of his great wisdom, riches, etc. <div eID="gen20927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20928" type="x-p"/> All nations shalt serve him - All the surrounding nations. This and the preceding verses are fully explained by <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.23-1Kgs.10.25">1Kgs 10:23-25</reference> : "King Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches and for wisdom. And all the earth sought unto Solomon to hear his wisdom. And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments and armor, and spices, horses and mules a rate year by year." If we take these expressions to mean literally all the habitable globe, then they cannot be applied to Solomon; but if we take them as they are most evidently used by the sacred writer, then they are literally true. When all the earth shall be brought to receive the Gospel of Christ, then they may be applied to him.
entries.041e24214d6778b035e99ff2e4c2339d1f05819e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20929" type="x-p"/> He shall deliver the needy when he crieth - The poor and the rich shall, in the administration of justice, be equally respected; and the strong shall not be permitted to oppress the weak.
entries.e28b4b6e7af51b13f35baa99812a8ad61ce2b2be: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20930" type="x-p"/> From deceit and violence - Because they are poor and uneducated, they are liable to be deceived; and because they are helpless, they are liable to oppression; but his equal justice shall duly consider these cases; and no man shall suffer because he is deceived, though the letter of the law may be against him. <div eID="gen20930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20931" type="x-p"/> And precious shall their blood be - If the blood or life of such a person shall have been spilt by the hand of violence, he shall seek it out, and visit it on the murderer, though he were the chief in the land. He shall not be screened, though he were of the blood royal, if he have willfully taken away the life of a man.
entries.c3e7a4805391eaf07462eb1eef2e86a166ba7d99: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen20931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20932" type="x-p"/> To him shall be given of the gold of Sheba - The Arabians shall pay him tribute. <div eID="gen20932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20933" type="x-p"/> Prayer also shall be made for him continually - In all conquered countries two things marked the subjection of the people: <div eID="gen20933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20934" type="x-p"/> 1. Their money was stamped with the name of the conqueror. <div eID="gen20934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20935" type="x-p"/> 2. They were obliged to pray for him in their acts of public worship. <div eID="gen20935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20936" type="x-p"/> Daily shall he be praised - He shall not act by the conquered like conquerors in general: he shall treat them with benignity; and shall give them the same laws and privileges as his natural subjects, and therefore "he shall be daily praised." All shall speak well of him.
entries.a998278ab40e42c2ba2bc3507bab2d73a34c1f2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20937" type="x-p"/> There shall be a handful of corn - The earth shall be exceedingly fruitful. Even a handful of corn sown on the top of a mountain shall grow up strong and vigorous; and it shall be, in reference to crops in other times as the cedars of Lebanon are to common trees or shrubs: and as the earth will bring forth in handfuls, so the people shall be multiplied who are to consume this great produce. <div eID="gen20937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20938" type="x-p"/> And they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth - There have been many puzzling criticisms concerning this verse. What I have given I believe to be the sense.
entries.8a4de948d0d3c27a90b6b6089383968d8a34e7af: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20939" type="x-p"/> His name shall endure for ever - Hitherto this has been literally fulfilled. Solomon is celebrated in the east and in the west, in the north and in the south; his writings still remain, and are received, both by Jews and by Gentiles, as a revelation from God; and it is not likely that the name of the author shall ever perish out of the records of the world. <div eID="gen20939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20940" type="x-p"/> All nations shall call him blessed - Because of the extraordinary manner in which he was favored by the Most High. I well know that all these things are thought to belong properly to Jesus Christ; and, in reference to him, they are all true, and ten thousand times more than these. But I believe they are all properly applicable to Solomon: and it is the business of the commentator to find out the literal sense, and historical fact, and not seek for allegories and mysteries where there is no certain evidence of their presence. Where the sacred writers of the New Testament quote passages from the Old, and apply them to our Lord, we not only may but should follow them. And I am ready to grant there may be many other passages equally applicable to him with those they have quoted, which are not thus applied. Indeed, He is the sum and substance of the whole Scripture. His spoke by his Spirit in the prophets; and himself was the subject of their declarations. See our Lord's saying, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.44">Luk 24:44</reference>.
entries.212f9bfa123805f5bd8adba565e92d63437e47ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20941" type="x-p"/> Blessed be the Lord God - David foresaw all Solomon's grandeur; his justice equity, and the happiness of the subjects under his government; and his soul has, in consequence, sensations of pleasure and gratitude to God, which even his own wondrous pen cannot describe. But it is worthy of remark, that God did not reveal to him the apostasy of this beloved son. He did not foresee that this once holy, happy, wise, and prosperous man would be the means of debasing the Divine worship, and establishing the grossest idolatry in Israel. God hid this from his eyes, that his heart might not be grieved, and that he might die in peace. Besides, there was still much contingency in the business. God would not predict a thing as absolutely certain, which was still poised between a possibility of being and not being; the scale of which he had left, as he does all contingencies, to the free-will of his creature to turn. <div eID="gen20941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20942" type="x-p"/> Who only doeth wondrous things - God alone works miracles: wherever there is a miracle there is God. No creature can invert or suspend the course and laws of nature; this is properly the work of God. Jesus Christ, most incontrovertibly, wrought such miracles; therefore, most demonstrably, Jesus Christ is God.
entries.fa9fe84975b45fb2e9101e4e48b838e9ead6b75e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20943" type="x-p"/> Let the whole earth be filled with his glory - Let the Gospel - the light, the Spirit, and power of Christ, fill the world. <div eID="gen20943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20944" type="x-p"/> Amen - So let it be. <div eID="gen20944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20945" type="x-p"/> And Amen - So it shall be. Hallelujah!
entries.d7b84193ec77dc4b25dd87add51d46261b327df9: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20946" type="x-p"/> The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended - This was most probably the last Psalm he ever wrote. There may be several in the after part of this book which were written by him; but they were probably composed in a former period of his life, for this was the end of the poetic prayers of David the son of Jesse. Those that were found afterwards have got out of their proper connection.  <chapter eID="Ps.72"/> <div eID="gen20946" type="x-p"/>

entries.d9cecf9949d6318a7089ab026be51d581c07df8c: <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1-Ps.72.4">Psa 72:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9721" type="x-p"/> The name of God, occurring only once, is <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>; and this is sufficient to stamp the Psalm as an Elohimic Psalm. מלך (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.2">Psa 21:2</reference>) and בּן־מלך are only used without the article according to a poetical usage of the language. The petition itself, and even the position of the words, show that the king’s son is present, and that he is king; God is implored to bestow upon him His משׁפּטים, i.e., the rights or legal powers belonging to Him, the God of Israel, and צדקה, i.e., the official gift in order that he may exercise those rights in accordance with divine righteousness. After the supplicatory teen the futures which now follow, without the <hi type="italic">Waw apodoseos</hi>, are manifestly optatives. Mountains and hills describe synecdochically the whole land of which they are the high points visible afar off. נשׂא is used in the sense of נשׂא פּרי <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.8">Eze 17:8</reference> : may שׁלום be the fruit which ripens upon every mountain and hill; universal prosperity satisfied and contented within itself. The predicate for <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference></hi> is to be taken from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference></hi>, just as, on the other hand, בּצדקה, “in or by righteousness,” the fruit of which is indeed peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa 32:17</reference>), belongs also to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference></hi>; so that consequently both members supplement one another. The wish of the poet is this: By righteousness, may there in due season be such peaceful fruit adorning all the heights of the land. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference></hi>, however, always makes one feel as though a verb were wanting, like תּפרחנה suggested by Böttcher. In <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">Psa 72:4</reference> the wishes are continued in plain unfigurative language. הושׁיע in the signification to save, to obtain salvation for, has, as is frequently the case, a dative of the object. בּני־אביון are those who are born to poverty, just like בּן־מלך, one who is born a king. Those who are born to poverty are more or less regarded, by an unrighteous government, as having no rights.
entries.c9e641102e987ca45f06363beede28c37b6915f0: <reference osisRef="Ps.72.5-Ps.72.8">Psa 72:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen9721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9722" type="x-p"/> The invocation of <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1">Psa 72:1</reference> is continued in the form of a wish: may they fear Thee, Elohim, עם־שׁמשׁ, with the sun, i.e., during its whole duration (עם in the sense of contemporary existence, as in Dan. 3:33). לפני־ירח, in the moonlight (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.8.16">Job 8:16</reference>, לפני־שׁמשׁ, in the sunshine), i.e., so long as the moon shines. דּור דּורים (accusative of the duration of time, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.102.25">Psa 102:25</reference>), into the uttermost generation which outlasts the other generations (like שׁמי השּׁמים of the furthest heavens which surround the other heavens). The first two periphrastic expressions for unlimited time recur in Psa 89:37., a Psalm composed after the time of Solomon; cf. the unfigurative expression in Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple in 1Ki 8:40. The continuance of the kingship, from the operation of which such continuance of the fear of God is expected, is not asserted until Psa 72:17. It is capricious to refer the language of address in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.5">Psa 72:5</reference> to the king (as Hupfeld and Hitzig do), who is not directly addressed either in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">Psa 72:4</reference>, or in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference>, or anywhere in the Psalm. With respect to God the desire is expressed that the righteous and benign rule of the king may result in the extension of the fear of God from generation to generation into endless ages. The poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference> delights in a heaping up of synonyms in order to give intensity to the expression of the thoughts, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.5">Psa 72:5</reference>; the last two expressions stand side by side one another without any bond of connection as in Psa 72:5. רביבים (from רבב, Arab. <hi type="italic">rbb , densum , spissum esse</hi>, and then, starting from this signification, sometimes <hi type="italic">multum</hi> and sometimes <hi type="italic">magnum esse</hi>) is the shower of rain pouring down in drops that are close together; nor is זרזיף a synonym of גּז, but (formed from זרף, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḏrf</hi>, to flow, by means of a rare reduplication of the first two letters of the root, Ew. §157, <hi type="italic">d</hi>) properly the water running from a roof (cf. <hi type="italic">B. Joma</hi> 87 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: “when the maid above poured out water, זרזיפי דמיא came upon his head”). גּז, however, is not the meadow-shearing, equivalent to a shorn, mown meadow, any more than גּז, גּזּה, Arabic <hi type="italic">ǵizza</hi>, signifies a shorn hide, but, on the contrary, a hide with the wool or feathers (e.g., ostrich feathers) still upon it, rather a meadow, i.e., grassy plain, that is intended to be mown. The closing word ארץ (<hi type="italic">accus. loci</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.147.15">Psa 147:15</reference>) unites itself with the opening word ירד: <hi type="italic">descendat in terram</hi>. In his last words (2 Sam. 23) David had compared the effects of the dominion of his successor, whom he beheld as by vision, to the fertilizing effects of the sun and of the rain upon the earth. The idea of <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference> is that Solomon’s rule may prove itself thus beneficial for the country. The figure of the rain in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">Psa 72:7</reference> gives birth to another: under his rule may the righteous blossom (expanding himself unhindered and under the most favourable circumsntaces), and (may there arise) salvation in all fulness עד־בּלי ירח, until there is no more moon (cf. the similar expression in <reference osisRef="Job.14.12">Job 14:12</reference>). To this desire for the uninterrupted prosperity and happiness of the righteous under the reign of this king succeeds the desire for an unlimited extension of his dominion, Psa 72:8. The sea (the Mediterranean) and the river (the Euphrates) are geographically defined points of issue, whence the definition of boundary is extended into the unbounded. Solomon even at his accession ruled over all kingdoms from the Euphrates as far as the borders of Egypt; the wishes expressed here are of wider compass, and Zechariah repeats them predictively (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>) with reference to the King Messiah.
entries.f406358cd7ecf243c87c92516d8f765fae4982dd: <reference osisRef="Ps.72.9-Ps.72.11">Psa 72:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen9722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9723" type="x-p"/> This third strophe contains prospects, the ground of which is laid down in the fourth. The position of the futures here becomes a different one. The contemplation passes from the home relations of the new government to its foreign relations, and at the same time the wishes are changed into hopes. The awe-commanding dominion of the king shall stretch even into the most distant corners of the desert. ציּים is used both for the animals and the men who inhabit the desert, to be determined in each instance by the context; here they are men beyond all dispute, but in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Isa 23:13</reference>, it is matter of controversy whether men or beasts are meant. Since the lxx, Aquila, Symmachus, and Jerome here, and the lxx and Jerome in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference>, render Αἰθίοπες, the nomadic tribes right and left of the Arabian Gulf seem traditionally to have been associated in the mind with this word, more particularly the so-called Ichthyophagi. These shall bend the knee reverentially before him, and those who contend against him shall be compelled at last to veil their face before him in the dust. The remotest west and south become subject and tributary to him, viz., the kings of Tartessus in the south of Spain, rich in silver, and of the islands of the Mediterranean and the countries on its coasts, that is to say, the kings of the Polynesian portion of Europe, and the kings of the Cushitish or of the Joktanitish שׁבא and of the Cushitish סבא, as, according to Josephus, the chief city of Meroë was called (vid., Genesis, S. 206). It was a queen of that Joktanitish, and therefore South Arabian <hi type="italic">Sheba</hi>, - perhaps, however, more correctly (vid., Wetzstein in my <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi>, ii. 529) of the Cushitish (Nubian) <hi type="italic">Sheba</hi>, - whom the fame of Solomon’s wisdom drew towards him, 1 Kings 10. The idea of their wealth in gold and in other precious things is associated with both peoples. In the expression השׁיב מנחה (to pay tribute, 2Ki 17:3, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.4">Psa 3:4</reference>) the tribute is not conceived of as rendered in return for protection afforded (Maurer, Hengstenberg, and Olshausen), nor as an act repeated periodically (Rödiger, who refers to <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.5">2Ch 27:5</reference>), but as a bringing back, i.e., repayment of a debt, <hi type="italic">referre s . reddere</hi> <hi type="italic">debitum</hi> (Hupfeld), after the same idea according to which obligatory incomings are called <hi type="italic">reditus</hi> (revenues). In the synonymous expression הקריב אשׁכּר the presentation appears as an act of sacrifice. אשׁכּר signifies in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference> a payment made in merchandise, here a rent or tribute due, from שׂכר, which in blending with the <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> <hi type="italic">prostheticum</hi> has passed over into שׂכר by means of a shifting of the sound after the Arabic manner, just as in אשׁכּל the verb שׂכל, to interweave, passes over into שׂכל (Rödiger in Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">Psa 72:11</reference> hope breaks through every bound: everything shall submit to his world-subduing sceptre.
entries.d36d139cd25dbb892257a1239a86c780c3e5045e: <reference osisRef="Ps.72.12-Ps.72.15">Psa 72:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen9723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9724" type="x-p"/> The confirmation of these prospects is now given. Voluntative forms are intermingled because the prospect extending into the future is nevertheless more lyrical than prophetic in its character. The elevation of the king to the dominion of the world is the reward of his condescension; he shows himself to be the helper and protecting lord of the poor and the oppressed, who are the especial object upon which God’s eye is set. He looks upon it as his task to deal most sympathizingly and most considerately (יחס) just with those of reduced circumstances and with the poor, and their blood is precious in his eyes. <reference osisRef="Ps.72.12">Psa 72:12</reference> is re-echoed in Job 29:12. The meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Psa 72:14</reference></hi> is the same as Psa 116:15. Instead of יקר, by a retention of the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> of the stem it is written ייקר. Just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Psa 49:10</reference>, ייקר here also is followed by ויחי. The assertion is individualized: and he (who was threatened with death) shall live (voluntative, having reference to the will of the king). But who is now the subject to ויתּן-? Not the rescued one (Hitzig), for after the foregoing designations (Psa 72:11.) we cannot expect to find “the gold of Sheba” (gold from Jeman or Aethiopia) in his possession. Therefore it is the king, and in fact Solomon, of whom the disposal of the gold of Sheba (Saba) is characteristic. The king’s thought and endeavour are directed to this, that the poor man who has almost fallen a victim shall live or revive, and not only will he maintain his cause, he will also bestow gifts upon him with a liberal hand, and he (the poor one who has been rescued and endowed from the riches of the king) shall pray unceasingly for him (the king) and bless him at all times. The poor one is he who is restored to life and endowed with gifts, and who intercedes and blesses; the king, however, is the beneficent giver. It is left for the reader to supply the right subjects in thought to the separate verbs. That clearly marked precision which we require in rhetorical recital is alien to the Oriental style (vid., my <hi type="italic">Geschichte der jüdischen Poesie</hi>, S. 189). Maurer and Hofmann also give the same interpretation as we have done.
entries.fe32db49e002add512feee5ac49e5a9df33bf1a8: <reference osisRef="Ps.72.16-Ps.72.17">Psa 72:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen9724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9725" type="x-p"/> Here, where the futures again stand at the head of the clauses, they are also again to be understood as optatives. As the blessing of such a dominion after God’s heart, not merely fertility but extraordinary fruitfulness may be confidently desired for the land פּסּה (ἁπ. λεγ..), rendered by the Syriac version <hi type="italic">sugo</hi>, abundance, is correctly derived by the Jewish lexicographers from פּסס = פּשׂה (in the law relating to leprosy), Mishnic פּסה, Aramaic פּסא, Arabic <hi type="italic">fšâ</hi>, but also <hi type="italic">fšš</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14-Ps.35.16">Psa 35:14-16</reference>), to extend, <hi type="italic">expandere</hi>; so that it signifies an abundance that occupies a broad space. בּראשׁ, unto the summit, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>; Psa 19:5. The idea thus obtained is the same as when Hofmann (<hi type="italic">Weissagung und Erfüllung</hi>, i. 180f.) takes פסּה (from פּסס = אפס) in the signification of a boundary line: “close upon the summit of the mountain shall the last corn stand,” with reference to the terrace-like structure of the heights. פּריו does not refer back to בארץ (Hitzig, who misleads one by referring to <reference osisRef="Joel.2.3">Joe 2:3</reference>), but to בּר: may the corn stand so high and thick that the fields, being moved by the wind, shall shake, i.e., wave up and down, like the lofty thick forest of Lebanon. The lxx, which renders huperarthee'setai, takes ירעשׁ for יראשׁ, as Ewald does: may its fruit rise to a summit, i.e., rise high, like Lebanon. But a verb ראשׁ is unknown; and how bombastic is this figure in comparison with that grand, but beautiful figure, which we would not willingly exchange even for the conjecture יעשׁר (may it be rich)! The other wish refers to a rapid, joyful increase of the population: may men blossom out of this city and out of that city as the herb of the earth (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.5.25">Job 5:25</reference>, where צאצאיך also accords in sound with יציצוּ), i.e., fresh, beautiful, and abundant as it. Israel actually became under Solomon’s sceptre as numerous “as the sand by the sea” (1Ki 4:20), but increase of population is also a settled feature in the picture of the Messianic time (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.20">Isa 49:20</reference>, Zec 2:8 [4]; cf. Sir. 44:21). If, however, under the just and benign rule of the king, both land and people are thus blessed, eternal duration may be desired for his name. May this name, is the wish of the poet, ever send forth new shoots (ינין <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi>), or receive new shoots (ינּון <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, from <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. ננון), as long as the sun turns its face towards us, inasmuch as the happy and blessed results of the dominion of the king ever afford new occasion for glorifying his name.
